raw_response:
I’m 58 this year, and with only one person in the house, I have to farm in a steady way, not chase fancy ideas. I’ve done this for 30 years in Quzhou, so I mostly follow what works here. Wheat-maize is still my backbone because it gives two harvests and keeps income safer. But cotton I still keep on part of the land, because if the price is decent it can bring cash. Cotton takes more picking labor, so with just me, I won’t plant too much of it. This year I’ll put **25 mu into wheat-maize rotation** and **15 mu into cotton**. For wheat and maize, I’ll use a moderate fertilizer rate, not the highest, because fertilizer and irrigation both cost money. I usually do a base application and then one topdressing. If the crop looks weak, I may add a little, but I won’t plan too much extra from the start. Since I have well irrigation, I can keep the key stages covered, but pumping water costs money, so I’ll irrigate mainly at the important times, not too often.

For wheat, I’ll sow in early October with a local improved variety people around here use, and I’ll aim for a solid stand before winter. I’ll plow and level the field after maize harvest, apply base fertilizer, and give wheat about three irrigations if the season is normal. After wheat harvest in June, I have to move fast into summer maize. That turnaround is always tight, so I’ll keep tillage simple and use rotary tillage or even direct sowing if time is short. Maize I’ll plant right after wheat comes off, use hybrid seed, and give enough nitrogen to keep the ears full, but not push too hard. Cotton I’ll plant on 15 mu in mid-April with improved seed. Cotton can make money, but it needs more labor for management and picking, so I’ll keep fertilizer moderate and watch pests closely, especially insects. My thinking this year is simple: protect the wheat-maize income first, keep some cotton for cash, and not spread myself too thin.
